content: The fifth edition of the Guidelines for Surveillance of Drug Resistance in Tuberculosis, published by the World Health Organization (WHO), provides updated recommendations for monitoring drug resistance in tuberculosis (TB). This document incorporates advancements in laboratory diagnostics, including molecular line probe assays and the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, which enable rapid detection of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB). It also reflects insights gained from 20 years of the Global Project on Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Resistance Surveillance, which has collected and analyzed data from 144 countries, representing 95% of the global population. The guidelines aim to assist national TB control programs (NTPs) in developing robust surveillance systems, starting with periodic surveys of sampled patients and progressing toward continuous surveillance through systematic drug susceptibility testing (DST). The ultimate goal is to establish routine, ongoing surveillance systems that provide reliable data on drug resistance patterns and trends over time. The document is divided into three parts: 1. Principles of Surveillance: This section outlines the foundational principles of the Global Project, emphasizing the importance of systematic and ongoing data collection to monitor drug resistance. Two main approaches are described: continuous surveillance based on routine DST of all TB patients and periodic surveys of sampled patients. Continuous surveillance is considered the gold standard but requires significant resources and infrastructure, which may not be available in all settings. 2. Planning and Implementing Surveys: This section provides detailed guidance on conducting surveys to estimate the burden of MDR-TB in specific areas. It includes steps for data collection, management, and interpretation, as well as recommendations for incorporating molecular technologies into surveillance systems. For countries with limited capacity for routine DST, periodic surveys remain a critical tool for estimating drug resistance patterns. 3. Monitoring Trends Over Time: This section discusses methods for tracking changes in drug resistance, particularly in countries with baseline data from previous surveys. Sentinel surveillance systems, which monitor trends in specific sites, are recommended as an interim approach for countries transitioning to routine surveillance. They also highlight the need for careful classification of patient treatment history, as previously treated patients are at higher risk of drug resistance. Surveillance data should be stratified by patient characteristics, such as age, sex, and HIV status, to identify risk groups and inform targeted interventions. The document includes updates from the 2009 edition, such as the integration of molecular technologies into surveys and the use of rapid molecular methods in sentinel sites to monitor trends. In resource-limited settings, periodic surveys are recommended every five years to provide critical information on the burden and distribution of drug resistance. These surveys can also strengthen laboratory capacity, transport systems, and data quality. However, they have limitations, such as the inability to detect localized outbreaks or provide continuous data. The guidelines stress the importance of collaboration with national HIV/AIDS programs when incorporating HIV testing into TB drug resistance surveillance. Overall, the guidelines serve as a comprehensive resource for NTPs, providing practical tools and strategies to enhance TB drug resistance surveillance and support global efforts to combat MDR-TB and XDR-TB.
